title: Understanding Web APIs
learning_outcomes: Explain what understanding web apis contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: api fundamentals.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: API integrations cross a network boundary where responses can be slow, malformed, unauthorized, duplicated, or unavailable. Check status and content, set timeouts, and make retries and webhook processing safe to repeat. In this lesson, focus on api fundamentals; then compare it with rest concepts. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use understanding web apis when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: API integrations cross a network boundary where responses can be slow, malformed, unauthorized, duplicated, or unavailable. Check status and content, set timeouts, and make retries and webhook processing safe to repeat. For understanding web apis, begin with api fundamentals. Also distinguish rest concepts; resources and representations; requests and responses. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

items.title: API fundamentals
items.text: Expect network failures and malformed responses; validate the response, set bounded timeouts, and make repeat delivery safe where needed.

items.title: REST concepts
items.text: Know when to use rest concepts, what input or program state it changes, and which boundary case is worth testing.

items.title: Requests and responses
items.text: Track where this value enters the request lifecycle and where it affects the response; client-provided data must be treated as untrusted.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Understanding Web APIs
content_blocks.code:
<?php
$json = "{\"items\":[1,2,3]}";
$payload = json_decode($json, true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
echo count($payload["items"]) . " items" . PHP_EOL;

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Set timeouts, validate remote responses, verify webhook authenticity, and make retries idempotent.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for understanding web apis from top to bottom. Start by identifying api fundamentals, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

The learner can explain its input, rule, and observable output.

hints: Start with the most direct listed subtopic and a single input.
Keep the example small enough that you can predict the output manually.
Test one normal case and one empty, invalid, or boundary case.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.

summary: Understanding Web APIs is one part of the PHP implementation workflow.
Prefer explicit behavior and testable examples over implicit assumptions.
Set timeouts, validate remote responses, verify webhook authenticity, and make retries idempotent.
